1:
The arrest interrupts a sermon, and the witnesses first establish who came. grammatical-historical Robertson explains that twenty-four bands of Levites guarded the temple, one on duty at a time, the commander of each band bearing this title, ranked by the Jewish historian next after the high priest. Lightfoot says the same from the rabbinic side, calling him captain of all the priestly and Levitical watches and citing the Talmudic title, ruler of the mountain of the house. Ellicott adds his rounds: as inspector he went by night, visited all the gates and roused the slumberers, so his presence implied the quiet order of the temple was thought to be endangered. Barnes places his guard chiefly in the tower Antonia during the great feasts and concludes the party came not as a mob but as keepers of the peace, expecting a tumult; though the verb for coming upon them implies suddenness and violence, which Robertson renders as bursting upon them or standing over them in hostility. eastern-antiochene Chrysostom sees a deliberate design in the choice of officer: the object was to attach a public criminality to what was being done, and not to prosecute it as the act of private individuals. reformed Calvin grants the form more than the others do. They have some show of law and equity, he says, for if any man intruded himself rashly it was the high priest’s office to repress him, to keep the people in obedience to the law and the prophets and to prevent all new doctrines; at first blush nothing here seems worthy of reprehension, and only the end declares their counsel wicked. He adds what the apostles thereby had to bear: being private and despised persons taking on public authority, they could not escape infamy, as the champions of Christ must swallow the same ignominy under the papacy.

Why the preaching provoked them is the second question. wesleyan-arminian Clarke makes it a matter of system: the whole Sadducean scheme was in danger from the preaching of the resurrection, since they believed neither in the immortality of the soul nor in any future world, and so made common cause with the priests. Ellicott adds motive to policy. The chief agents in the condemnation of Christ appear here for the first time in the book, congratulating themselves months later on the counsel they had followed and industriously circulating the report that the body had been stolen; and the shame of having been put to silence by Christ added vindictiveness to their calculation. Throughout the Acts, he observes, the Sadducees are foremost as persecutors while the Pharisees temporise or profess themselves believers. Barnes reads the grief as indignation and anger rather than sorrow, and locates its ground as much in the teachers as in the doctrine: unlearned Galileans unconnected with the priestly office presumed to instruct the people, and no inquiry was made whether the miracle had been wrought, the only question being whether they conformed to the authorities’ views of doctrine and order. Calvin puts it shortest — they hated the doctrine before they knew it. Clarke observes that their minds suffered more labour through vexation at the apostles’ success than the apostles’ bodies did in a whole day of preaching. Wesley finds the reason in their own guilt, since the rising proved him the Just One and brought his blood upon their heads, and reads the arrest as providential ordering, that the two should testify first in the temple and then in the great council, to which they could have had no access except as criminals. puritan-evangelical Henry draws the practical lesson: let Christ’s servants be ever so resolute, Satan’s agents will be spiteful, and therefore let Satan’s agents be ever so spiteful, Christ’s servants ought to be resolute. Gill notes that though only Peter’s preaching was recorded before, John doubtless preached as well.
3:
The custody is brief and the notes on it procedural. grammatical-historical Barnes explains that they were taken into safe keeping, probably under guard, and gives the reason for the delay: the council was not conveniently assembled at night, the hour being that of the evening sacrifice, when the sanhedrim did not usually convene. Robertson locates the ward in a chamber of the temple and draws the near comparison: no trial could take place before the next day, a regulation violated at Christ’s own trial. Ellicott fixes the clock: the narrative began at three in the afternoon and the eventide at six; the word for hold means custody, translated prison a chapter later, and survives in the modern stronghold. reformed Gill notes that one version has them seizing both by force and drawing them out of the temple.

The verse that follows reverses the scene, and the witnesses fasten on it. Barnes calls it one of the instances since so often repeated in which persecution has only extended the faith it was designed to destroy: it became a proverb that the blood of the martyrs is the seed of the church, and no lesson has been learnt so slowly as that persecution confirms men in their opinions. It was supposed here that the disciples were few, without power, wealth or influence, and easy to crush at once. puritan-evangelical Henry put the same at the head of the chapter: though the preachers were persecuted the word prevailed, for the church’s suffering days have sometimes been her growing days, and the days of her infancy were so. What the number means occupies the rest. Barnes thinks it improbable that five thousand were converted in the portico on a single cure, and takes the figure as the total who had joined the apostles to that point, including the hundred and twenty and the three thousand of Pentecost — still leaving an accession of near two thousand as proof of the presence of the Spirit. wesleyan-arminian Clarke does the arithmetic: the hundred and twenty before Pentecost, the three thousand at it, and one thousand eight hundred and eighty since; some think all five thousand were converted this day, but this is by no means likely, and the historian does not fix the number, since he writes about. Ellicott renders it that the number was made up to about five thousand, agrees that this is an aggregate rather than a day’s converts, and observes that women and children were not included, as in the feeding of the five thousand. He suggests the count was taken as it was there, by grouping those who came to baptism by hundreds and fifties, and that the coincidence could scarcely fail to make the disciples connect the two, so that as they broke the bread they felt they were giving men the true bread from heaven. Wesley makes the same connection independently in one line: beside women and children they were about five thousand, so many as our Lord now fed at once with the bread from heaven. Calvin understands the number not of those newly added but of the whole church, and finds the marvel elsewhere: the apostles are in prison, but the force of their preaching is spread far and wide and its course at liberty, so that a few unarmed men, furnished with no garrisons, show more power in their voice alone than all the world does in raging against them. That the faithful were not terrified by the danger and discouraged from taking up the cross he thinks the greater wonder, this being a hard beginning for novices; and Christ declared himself alive more evidently by this force of doctrine than if he had offered his body to be handled and seen. Clarke closes with what the others leave implicit: a goodly flock in one city, as the commencement of the Christian Church.
5:
The court is described in three words, and each is taken apart. grammatical-historical Robertson lists the three classes that composed the Sanhedrin — rulers, meaning the chief priests, who were Sadducees; scribes, usually Pharisees; and elders in neither class — numbering twenty-four, twenty-two and twenty-four. Barnes takes the elders for presbyters chosen from the people, and catches a turn of phrase: the writer says their rulers rather than ours, as though the book were composed for Gentile readers. Ellicott would repunctuate, since the last two words are misplaced in the English by being carried to the end of the next verse; and he judges the meeting summoned expressly to consider the new facts, probably the first formal sitting since the trial of Christ, and one including the Pharisee scribes as well as the Sadducees. Where they gathered is a question in itself. Barnes notes that Jerusalem was the usual place, but that Jewish writers say the council moved from place to place in the forty years before the city fell, so naming it here implies it sometimes met elsewhere — and he thinks the members were out of town the previous evening, which is why the trial was deferred. Lightfoot lays out both senses, the city against the country or the town against the temple, and prefers the first: they had come in from the adjacent towns, and may be supposed assembled for some solemnity of the day rather than merely to take cognizance of this case. He doubts they all even knew of the imprisonment, which was probably carried out in their absence by some chief of the priests, the captain of the watches and the Sadducees, and not by a just Sanhedrim.

How eager the court was divides two of them. puritan-evangelical Henry reads a slackening in the timing: they sat on the morrow and not in the night as when Christ was tried, so they seem not to have been so hot upon this prosecution, and it was well if they began to relent — though they adjourned no further than the morrow, being impatient to have the men silenced. He weighs the bench: the scribes were men of learning who came to dispute and hoped to confute, the rulers and elders men in power who, if they could not answer, thought they could find some cause to silence; and if the gospel had not been of God it could never have made its way, having both the learning and the power of the world against it. Jerusalem he counts an aggravation, for in the city where so many looked for redemption before it came, more would not look upon it when it did. reformed Calvin sees no relenting, only restraint. The wicked omit no subtilty to blot out the gospel and the name of Christ, and make an assembly in which everything is done so tyrannously that lust bears a show of right and the truth may seem condemned by good right; whatever the apostles bring in defence will remain buried within walls where none bears them any favour. But the Lord brings a sudden fear upon them, so that they dare not do what they can and most desire, and being held back by fear of the people they bridle their fury to avoid envy. He also enters a chronological difficulty the others meet only later: on the historian’s dating Caiaphas held the office some three years past the crucifixion, so either this sitting fell later than is supposed or, since the man who succeeded Caiaphas was the son of Annas, the son was called by his father’s name — and even so, he grants, the whole difficulty is not solved. wesleyan-arminian Clarke states only that these with the high priest formed the grand council of the Jews, and Wesley that the judges were eminent for power, wisdom and learning; Gill notes the custody overnight.
6:
Why the man named first is called the high priest is the puzzle of the verse. wesleyan-arminian Clarke says he was not then in office but had held it eleven years, bore the title all his life, and had the honour, unique since the Mosaic institution, of seeing five sons fill the place after him. grammatical-historical Robertson makes the distinction cleanly: Caiaphas was high priest by Roman law, Annas in Jewish opinion. Ellicott adds the dates — in office from the seventh to the fifteenth year, Caiaphas appointed in the seventeenth and deposed in the thirty-seventh — and suggests Annas kept a dominant influence for life, perhaps as President of the Sanhedrin, which would explain the title. reformed Gill offers two options, that he had been high priest or was the deputy with the other priests under his government, and is named first as father-in-law to Caiaphas; but he denies the presidency, since not Annas but Gamaliel presided then. Wesley states the bare fact, one having been high priest and the other being so now. The third name is as vexed. Lightfoot conjectures the famous rabbi of that generation, none in the nation being then more celebrated, and he of priestly stock, and cites the tradition that forty years before the destruction, when the temple gates flew open of themselves, he cried, O temple, temple, why dost thou disturb thyself? I know thy end, that thou shalt be destroyed. Clarke adopts the conjecture as highly probable. Ellicott calls the identification at best uncertain, but tells the death-bed story it makes available: asked why he wept, the old man answered that a king of flesh and blood he might soothe with words or appease with a gift, but he was to be brought before the King of kings, whose wrath and bonds are eternal, and two paths lay before him, one to Paradise and one to Gehenna, and he knew not which they would lead him. Of the fourth name Barnes says nothing is known, while Clarke and Ellicott identify him with a rich Jew of the period, brother to a famous philosopher. Clarke reads the last clause as of the race of the high priests, and notes that the names show how formidable were the enemies the infant Church faced.

The examination opens with a question, and its tone is read differently. Gill and Ellicott describe the chamber, the council sitting in a half circle rather than a full one, as the Jews put it like a half moon, so parties and witnesses might speak before them all, the accused set in the centre. Ellicott hears contempt in the form of words — by what kind of power, by what kind of name — and notes the imperfect, so that they were asking, putting it repeatedly in varying forms; they admit the cure as too patent to deny, but will not call it a sign or a wonder, only this. Clarke reads a legal trap: convinced the man was healed, they likely took the whole for magic, and since all intercourse with familiar spirits was unlawful they hoped the examination would bring it out and the disturbers of their peace be put to death — by what supernatural energy, in what mode of incantation, and who is the spirit you invoke? He allows the alternative that they demanded credentials. Robertson agrees the phrasing suggests a magical formula such as the exorcists practised, and marks the emphatic ye. Barnes sees intimidation: they assumed the men impostors, and it did not occur to them to ask whether the acknowledged miracle proved them sent from God. Calvin grants them a feigned zeal, dealing as though they were earnest defenders of God’s glory, while labouring by many questions on a manifest matter to wring a denial from them; but God brought their craft to nothing. Wesley says only that they seem ambiguous on purpose.
8:
What accounts for the change in the man is the first question. reformed Calvin says the note about the Spirit is added so we may know Peter did not speak with such majesty of himself: having denied his Master when frightened at the voice of a silly woman, he should have fainted in such an assembly at merely beholding their pomp, unless upheld by the Spirit. He had great need of wisdom and strength, and excels so much in both that his answer is indeed divine; he is another manner of man here than before. Two things follow: the doctrine to come is commended as having its origin in the Spirit, and we are taught to crave that Spirit whenever we make profession of our faith. grammatical-historical Barnes reads the contrast morally. Peter could not have forgotten that before this council his Master had been condemned, nor that in the very room where it met he had shrunk from an honest avowal and denied him; that he now stands boldly before the same tribunal proves the genuineness of the repentance in which he went out and wept bitterly, one evidence of which is the desire to repair the evil done — and here was the opportunity. Ellicott finds the tense decisive of a sudden inspiration, and catches a coincidence the others miss: on each side of the chamber stood a John, and on each a Cephas or Caiaphas, names possibly of one root and at any rate close in sound, so the new and the older Israel face each other under the same names. Gill dates the filling to that instant, a fresh measure beyond Pentecost; Clarke sees fulfilled the promise that they should take no thought how or what to speak; Robertson says only, for this occasion, above all fear. wesleyan-arminian Wesley gives the principle: God moves his instruments not when they please, but when he sees it needful. eastern-antiochene Cyril of Jerusalem sets the hour in a longer arc, tracing one power of the Spirit from the three thousand taken at Pentecost in the spiritual net of Peter’s words, through the healing at the Beautiful gate, to this hour in which, having taken five thousand believers at once, they confute the misguided rulers of the people.

How he opens divides them sharply. Barnes says he addressed the council with perfect respect and did not call their authority in question, treating the summons as an opportunity to state the evidence, on the principle he would afterwards lay down, that a man be always ready to give an answer with meekness and fear. Ellicott traces more deference in the Galilean fisherman’s address than in Paul’s words before the same court later, Paul being more familiar with its members and standing in less awe; and Wesley says simply that he gives them the honour due to their office. Calvin hears the opposite. Peter lays tyranny to the charge of the priests, because they examine him unjustly concerning a benefit that deserved praise, as though he had committed some heinous offence; and he answers the wicked affection of their minds rather than the order of their question. Had the apostles used a miracle to draw the people from the true worship of God they should worthily have been called to account, since religion far excels all the good things of this life; but seeing these men made an offence of what they ought to have honoured, Peter girds them wittily for sitting as judges to condemn good deeds — though he touches it lightly and passes on. Robertson catches the same move: a benefactor, not a malefactor, a skilful turn made by Peter. Ellicott adds that the word for good deed is strictly an act of beneficence, set against the contemptuous this thing of the question, and that made whole carries a pregnant sense of spiritual as well as bodily restoration.
10:
The answer names the name, and the witnesses weigh the cost. grammatical-historical Barnes says Peter might have evaded the question, as Calvin observed before him, but chose to state his conviction fully before the great and the mighty. He calls it a striking illustration of the fitness of the name the Lord gave him, the vacillating Simon transformed into the decided Cephas, and holds the change cannot be accounted for except on the supposition that the religion is true, Peter having no worldly motive and the disciples’ hopes of honour lying buried with Jesus. reformed Calvin gives the reason the starting-holes were refused: the miracle was wrought that the name of Christ might be glorified, so the wicked, will they, nill they, must hear what they would have buried full deep. He sets out the order of the argument: Christ is made author of the miracle, and then, since it seemed absurd that a dead man be endued with divine power, his life is testified from the raising, so the miracle becomes an occasion for preaching the resurrection. wesleyan-arminian Clarke keeps to the evidence: the cure was notorious, the infirmity long known, the man standing before them sound, so they could judge it themselves. Robertson calls the charge too good a chance to miss, marks the emphatic ye, and hears a play on one word — in this one this one stands, a centre shot. Ellicott presses the clause: though Pilate gave the formal sentence, it was they who crucified their King. Wesley notes what they did not do: they knew in their consciences it was so, and though they had hired the soldiers to tell a senseless tale, they never dared plead it before Peter and John. Calvin adds that the charge is laid not merely to upbraid them but that they may know they strove against God in vain.

The quotation they had heard before. Lightfoot puts the difficulty plainly. Are these things said of the Messiah? The Jew will hardly believe his pompous Messiah should be rejected by his own countrymen, and therefore does Peter the more vehemently inculcate it. They had often recited the words in their Great Hallel, but you shall never persuade them these things were spoken of their Messiah, rather of Jacob, David, or the congregation of Israel. Barnes confirms it, the ancient reading applying the verse to the child among Jesse’s sons worthy to be made king, while the New Testament writers apply it to the Messiah — and draws the lesson that what men set at nought God esteems of inestimable value. Calvin traces the double reference: David complains he is rejected by the captains of the people yet boasts that God chose him for the chief room, and what was shadowed in David God expressed perfectly in the Messiah. He reads the citation as a check on office, made lest the elders and priests, puffed up with their honour, take liberty to allow or disallow whatever they would; and it must be fulfilled daily, so it seems no new thing if the chief builders reject Christ now — whereby, he adds, the boasting of the papacy is refuted, its claim going no further than to be chief builders with Annas and Caiaphas. Ellicott makes the builders their own calling: they built the Church of Israel and rejected the stone God chose, on which the walls of Jew and Gentile meet and are bonded; thirty years later the thought still dominates Peter’s epistles. Robertson calls them the experts, the architects, and leaves open whether the head of the corner is the highest stone under the roof or the stone beneath the building. Clarke draws the inference: one part of their own prophecy being so literally fulfilled in the rejection, they may rest assured the other shall be. Gill takes the stone for the Messiah, comparable to one for strength and duration.
12:
The move from the cure to salvation is the pivot of the speech. grammatical-historical Barnes traces the word from its general sense of keeping anything safe to its use for the work the Messiah came to do, and gives two reasons for the turn: the healed man’s deliverance suggested the greater deliverance from sin and death that the same power effects, and the occasion was favourable for setting the doctrine before the council — the more so since Peter advanced a sentiment he expected them to concur in, that salvation is to be had only by the Messiah. Ellicott says the pregnant force of the earlier verb for being made whole comes out at its highest, so the salvation proclaimed is not from bodily infirmity but from the great disease of sin; and he notes the article, since Peter names the salvation the rulers professed to look for. wesleyan-arminian Wesley calls it a beautiful gradation from the temporal deliverance of a cripple to a nobler kind wrought for sinful souls, Peter following the custom of his Master, who continually took occasion from earthly things to speak of spiritual. reformed Calvin describes the same passage from the corporal benefit to perfect health, and says Christ showed this token that he might be known as the only author of life. He also hears a sting: the priests, who had gone about to put the name of Christ out of remembrance, are twice damned, since they not only refused the salvation offered but endeavoured to bring it to nothing and take its use from the people. And though Peter seems to speak to deaf men, he preaches the grace of Christ still, if any can bear to hear, and if not, that they may be left without excuse.

How far the exclusive clause reaches divides two of them. Ellicott extends it beyond those who hear the name. To those to whom it has been made known the Name is the one true source of deliverance, and Peter, speaking for himself and the rulers, rightly says it is the name whereby we must be saved; but where it is not so known, he holds, it rises to a higher significance as the symbol of a divine energy, so that we may rightly say the heathen who obtain salvation are saved by the Name of a Lord of whom they never heard. Robertson allows no such extension. It is amazing, he says, to see Peter speaking thus to the Sanhedrin and proclaiming the necessity of salvation in the name of Jesus Christ and no other; if that was true then it is true today, and there is no second name to set beside it in India, China, Japan or America. Clarke stands nearer Robertson: not only no other person but no name except the divinely appointed one, and no other means ever devised by God, all others being subordinate and having their efficacy from him alone, the Lamb slain from the foundation of the world. Gill lists what is excluded rather than what is included: salvation is not in a man’s self nor in any creature, angels or men, not in his own works and legal righteousness, not by obedience to the law of Moses, not by the light of nature, much less by the traditions of the elders. Calvin grounds the exclusiveness in the decree: salvation is in Christ alone because God decreed it so, and since it is in God’s power only he will not have it made common to us by any other means than asking it of Christ. He adds why the clause is framed as it is: men cannot ascend into heaven to come to God, and being so far from his kingdom it was needful that God not only invite us but reach out his hand and offer salvation, which he did in sending Christ down to bring it.
13:
Two Greek words describe the men in the dock, and all say they are misread. wesleyan-arminian Clarke is bluntest: the first means persons without literature, the second persons in private life; it does not mean ignorance in the common acceptation, and the English rendering is very improper, for in no sense could any apostle be called ignorant — their spiritual knowledge came all from heaven, but in all else they were men of good, sound, strong common sense. grammatical-historical Robertson makes the distinction technical: unlettered men without training in the rabbinical schools, as Jesus himself was reckoned; and the second a layman, not in office, a common soldier and not an officer — men of ability and courage who did not belong to the set of the rabbis. Ellicott sharpens the first by the sense of letters among the Jews, whence the scribes took their name, so it means not educated as a scribe; and he follows the second down the centuries: the Latin version reproduced rather than translated it, whence it passed into the modern languages with ignorance attached and acquired its later sense of idiot. Barnes keeps the older reading, of men without education or practice in public speaking, and adds that Galileans were regarded as particularly rude and uncultivated. Wesley takes the fact rather than the word: by such men, though not by such only, has God in all ages caused his word to be preached.

How they recognised the two is the second question. Ellicott and Robertson press the imperfect: they began to recognise, one ruler after another remembering the two apostles as they had seen them with their Master in the Temple. Clarke agrees that they had probably often seen the Lord teaching with these disciples attending him. Barnes will not say how the evidence was obtained, but supposes it came from the miracle, the bold declaration, and the conviction that none would be so bold who had not been with Christ; their boldness, he adds, owed nothing to the arts of rhetoric. reformed Calvin reads the recognition as self-conviction. Here may we see an evil conscience: destitute of right and reason, they break into the tyranny whose hatred they had tried to escape. Knowing the two unlearned, they acknowledge somewhat more than belongs to man in their boldness, and are enforced to wonder whether they will or no; when they confess the sign manifest they condemn themselves of an evil conscience, and when they say it is known to all men they declare that, passing over God, they have respect to men only — betraying that they would have turned their backs had there been any colour of denial. Barnes glosses the boldness as openness in speaking, opposed to hesitancy and equivocation; Robertson renders it telling it all, and observes that Peter had turned the table on the Sanhedrin and arraigned them before the bar of God. Ellicott notes that John, so far as we read, had not spoken, but look and bearing showed he shared the courage; that this boldness of speech had marked his Lord’s teaching and now became the disciples’ distinctive mark; and that the beloved disciple uses the word not of boldness toward men but of confidence toward God. On the healed man standing there they converge. Barnes calls his presence an unanswerable fact, so public that no evasion remained, and thinks it evinced no little gratitude; Gill has him coming of his own accord as a witness. Clarke sets it out as a syllogism: if the doctrine be false the man cannot have been miraculously healed, and if healed the doctrine must be true; but he is incontestably healed, therefore the doctrine is true. Robertson has the court still with nothing to say against it; Calvin asks the question that ends the scene: after they have put two simple men to silence, shall the arm of God be broken?
15:
The prisoners are put outside and the court confers, and the witnesses read the conference differently. grammatical-historical Robertson pictures it plainly: with Peter and John and the lame man out of the room, they began to compare notes and take stock of their predicament. Barnes reckons the options before them — death, imprisonment, scourging, or the mere exertion of their authority — and says fear of the multitude deterred them from the first three, so that they fell back on a command and supposed it would be enough. He notes that before this same body and probably these same men the Saviour had been arraigned, and before them Peter had denied him; the memory of the disciples’ flight and of that denial may well have persuaded the council that a threat would deter them now. It did not: on the next occasion they added beating to their threats. Ellicott states the objection to the whole proceeding. The question they debated ought never to have been asked at all, since they were sitting as a court of justice and should have given a verdict for or against the accused according to the evidence; instead they abandon that office and begin discussing what policy was most expedient — which he observes was characteristic of Caiaphas. puritan-evangelical Henry answers the question they asked. If they would have yielded to the convincing and commanding power of truth it had been easy to say what they should do to these men: they should have placed them at the head of their council, received their doctrine, been baptized by them in the name of the Lord Jesus and joined in fellowship with them. But when men will not be persuaded to do what they should do, it is no marvel that they are at a loss what to do; the truths of Christ, entertained as they should be, would give no manner of trouble, but held in unrighteousness they become a burdensome stone.

What their own admission amounts to is the second point. Ellicott hears more in it than an admission: the very form of the sentence, he says, betrays the will, though there is not the power. Robertson reduces it to calculation — it will do no good to deny it, useless with the man standing there. wesleyan-arminian Clarke states the evidence that closed the door: all Jerusalem knew the man had been lame from his birth and had long begged at the Beautiful gate, and now all Jerusalem knew that he was healed, so that there was no means by which such a self-evident fact could be disproved. Barnes calls it simply a known and undeniable miracle, and observes that their whole object was not to deny the fact but to prevent the use the apostles were plainly making of it, to convince the people that Jesus was the Messiah. reformed Gill lists what they weighed — whether to scourge, to detain longer in custody, to imprison, or to dismiss — and notes that the order to withdraw may have taken the healed man out with the two apostles. Henry marks what the withdrawal was for: they were willing enough to be rid of men who spoke so home to their consciences, and unwilling that the prisoners should hear the acknowledgements which were extorted from them — though, he adds, if the men might not hear them, we have them here upon record, since the designs of Christ’s enemies are carried on in close cabals and they dig deep, as if they would hide their counsels from the Lord. He also reads the whole trial as a graded schooling: the apostles came off now with flying colours, because they must be trained up to sufferings by degrees and prepared by lesser trials for greater; they now but run with the footmen, and hereafter we shall have them contending with horses.
17:
What they fear will spread is not the news but the doctrine. wesleyan-arminian Clarke says so explicitly: not the report of the cure, which was already everywhere, but the teaching of these men; more than a thousand had professed faith in consequence of the miracle, and if the teaching went on they had reason to believe all Jerusalem would be converted to the religion of him they had lately crucified. reformed Gill draws the line geographically: the fame had covered the city, and it was the rest of the nation they meant to protect. Wesley puts their view in a phrase: they look on it as a mere gangrene, and so does all the world upon genuine Christianity. Why the enmity is so implacable is the harder question. grammatical-historical Lightfoot sets the case beside another. All men esteemed John the Baptist a prophet, and they did not so much oppugn his preaching; why then set themselves so against the preaching of Jesus, signalized with far greater miracles? His answer is that the fathers of the Sanhedrim had a downright knowledge, or at least a suspicion, that Jesus was the Messiah, and from this arose their hatred. Clarke reaches the same place by another road: nothing was so ominous to them as the name of Christ crucified, because they had been his crucifiers and could not bear to hear salvation preached through the man they had murdered. Robertson catches the recoil in the wording: they will not say the name but slur at this name, though they do bring themselves to say Jesus in the command that follows. Ellicott finds the command more forcible still: the Greek is absolutely not to utter, so the very name of Jesus was not to pass their lips. Wesley marks the two halves of the ban: not to speak privately nor teach publicly.

The idiom of the threat carries a question about the record. Ellicott gives the literal form, let us threaten them with threats, and identifies the Hebrew way of expressing intensity by reduplication; so far as it goes, this indicates the writer translated a report of a speech delivered in Aramaic — though he allows the alternative that the high priest, speaking Greek, reproduced the old formula as the Greek Old Testament does. Clarke takes the same evidence without the alternative, calling it proof that the council’s words were translated into Greek just as spoken. Barnes notes only that the construction is a Hebraism of intensity, and that the threat took the form of a command with an unstated displeasure behind it. Robertson keeps to the grammar, marking the hortatory subjunctive, the middle voice and the double negative of the indirect command. reformed Calvin draws from it a rule about office. Here may we see what a deadly evil power void of the fear of God is, for where reverence does not reign, the more holy the place a man possesses the more boldly he rages; and for that cause we should take good heed that the wicked be not preferred to the government of the Church, while those called to it must behave modestly, lest they seem armed to do hurt. But if they abuse their honour, he says, the Spirit declares here as in a glass how small an account we ought to make of their decrees: pastoral authority has certain bounds appointed which it may not pass, and if they dare be so bold we may lawfully refuse to obey. Clarke turns the ban into a test of the doctrine: any other name the hypocrite will bear, but the doctrine according to godliness, proclaiming salvation through the blood of Christ crucified, they will not bear — and if it were not the truth of God it could not be so unpopular. Wesley answers the court: great men, ye do nothing, for they have a greater than you to flee to.
19:
The answer states a principle, and how far it reaches is the chapter’s largest question. grammatical-historical Barnes calls it one of the first and boldest appeals on record for the right of private judgment: responsibility for religious opinion is direct to God, and other men have no power of control, the opposite being tyranny. He notes the court could not resist the appeal, since it acknowledged it had no authority except by divine appointment and could not deny that it is better to obey God than man; the only question left was whether God had commanded here, of which the apostles were satisfied. reformed Calvin presses harder because of who was answered. This council did undoubtedly represent the Church, and yet, because they abuse their authority, the apostles say flatly they are not to be obeyed; obedience rendered to evil pastors, however lawfully they hold the government of the Church, is contrary to God. By what title soever men be called, we must hear them only on this condition, that they lead us not away from obeying God, so all their traditions must be examined by the rule of the Word; and if such modesty is required in civil government, where princes must be obeyed yet not so as to rob God of his right, it holds far more in the Church. Ellicott grants the axiom and qualifies it. In theory the right is self-evident, but in practice the difficulty is whether the divine authority claimed is really there, and the only answer is that men who believe they have it are bound to act as if they had. Where the question is one of witness to facts they must not tamper with the truth for fear of offending men; but as men pass from facts to doctrines, and from opinions to conjectures, the duty of not saying what they do not believe remains while the obligation to proclaim does not, and there are cases where reticence is right as well as politic. The burden of proof rests on the man who asserts the higher authority: intensity of conviction may be enough for himself but cannot satisfy others, and one who refuses to debate on the ground of reason and conscience because he is certain he is right is convicted of an almost insane egotism.

Why they could not be silent is answered alike. Barnes finds a necessity laid on them by the evidence received and the direct command to preach; Ellicott marks the emphatic pronoun, we for our part, and observes that the question at issue was one of bearing witness, which they had a special command to bear. wesleyan-arminian Clarke puts it as the apostles might: worldly prudence and our secular interests would induce us to obey you, but acting before God we dare not be silent, and we should be guilty of treason were we to suppress his testimony. Robertson calls the reply a justified defiance, since the temple rulers had stepped in between the conscience and God, and the two were willing to pay the price with their lives — the courage of martyrs in every age. Gill notes only that the impossibility was moral, not physical. Calvin enters the caution Ellicott entered above. Many things found by hearing and seeing may and even ought to be concealed when the question is the redeeming of peace, since it is wicked stubbornness to raise a tumult about unnecessary matters; but the apostles do not speak generally, for the gospel is in hand, wherein consists both the glory of God and the salvation of men, and whoever puts them to silence endeavours to abolish the grace of God. Wesley reaches for a pagan parallel, the philosopher who told his Athenian judges that he loved them but would obey God rather than them, and would die a thousand times rather than buy his life by ceasing to teach.
21:
The release is a defeat, and it is accounted for in three ways. grammatical-historical Barnes puts it down to fear of a tumult: they could devise no way of punishing the two without exciting the people and endangering their own authority, and the council was often so influenced, which shows how much its power hung on the caprice of the multitude. wesleyan-arminian Clarke makes the calculation more precise. The people had seen the miracle, confessed the finger of God, and believed, and the converts were by now so numerous that the council feared an insurrection; he notes too a manuscript reading that turns the clause into finding no cause why they might punish them, which he reports as better sense and better Greek. reformed Calvin allows the human cause and looks past it. How is it, he asks, that being content with threatenings they do not rage against the apostles’ bodies, save only because the power of God binds them as a chain? Not that the fear of God prevails with them, for regard of the people alone hinders them; but the Lord binds them, though they are ignorant of it, and the providence by which he preserves his children, hidden from the wicked, is beheld by the eyes of faith. He finds a further irony: the priests assemble, not without great rumour, all men wait for some rare event, and the apostles depart acquitted, so the adversaries are not only vanquished but confirm the gospel against their will. Yet the victory is not unmixed, for the faithful are always humbled under the cross: they are threatened again, and so do not triumph except under its reproach. Clarke observes that the further threatening means new penalties appended to the old, and Robertson glosses the same prefix; Gill supposes they repeated the old threats or added sharper ones, not being able to answer the arguments.

What the people’s praise proves is the second. Barnes takes it for the highest evidence of the miracle’s reality: even the council, with all its prejudice, never called it in question, and the people, who had known the man for years, were convinced it was real — and it would have been impossible to impose thus on keen-sighted and jealous adversaries. Robertson presses the tense for its irony: they kept on glorifying God while the council still threatened, which was to laugh at the helplessness of the court. Ellicott marks the same continued action and finds it characteristic of this writer to record the impression signs made on the people. Wesley draws what the others leave unsaid: the people were so much wiser than those set over them. Calvin will not grant so much. He calls the praise the fruit of the miracle a second time, but doubts all were brought to the perfect end, since a man touched with the power of God who does not come to Christ stays midway; yet it was something, though not all, that the power of God was acknowledged, so the adversaries were ashamed and gave back. On the man’s age the notes converge, then diverge in application. Barnes says the forty years show the greatness of the cure, since after so long all hope of healing by ordinary means must have been abandoned and any pretence of jugglery absurd; Gill adds that the man was better known and his testimony met with more credit. Ellicott finds the same precision about the duration of a disease elsewhere in his two books. Clarke turns it to the reader: the disease was of long standing and the more inveterate, but all difficulties yield equally to the sovereign power of God, and it is as easy to convert a sinner of fourscore as one of ten — though he who refuses the call now has neither reason nor revelation to support a hope of receiving hereafter the salvation he rejects today.
23:
Where they went and why they told it are the two questions. grammatical-historical Ellicott reads their own people as implying a recognised place of meeting where the new society came together at fixed times, and takes the chief priests in the wider sense, taking in not only Annas and Caiaphas but the heads of the four-and-twenty courses. Robertson agrees the phrase means the whole brotherhood and not the apostles only, and draws an inference the others do not: for all Peter’s defiance, the two told the company everything that had been said, and they had real apprehension of the outcome. puritan-evangelical Henry makes their return a lesson twice over. Though God had highly honoured them and enabled them to acquit themselves so well, they were not puffed up nor thought themselves above their brethren — and no advancement in gifts or usefulness should set us above either the duties or the privileges of the communion of saints. And though their enemies had endeavoured to break their knot and frighten them from the work, they returned without fearing the wrath of their rulers; they might have had comfort in retiring to their closets, but they were men in a public station and had to seek the public good rather than their own satisfaction, for Christ’s followers do best in company, provided it be their own. wesleyan-arminian Clarke supplies the scene: this was properly the first persecution against the Church since the resurrection, and the rest of the disciples, knowing of the imprisonment and the temper of the rulers, had doubtless been making joint supplication for their safety, in which employment the two found them.

Why the report was made divides them. eastern-antiochene Chrysostom denies any thought of self: not for their own glory did they tell the tale, but what they displayed was the proofs therein exhibited of the grace of Christ. All that their adversaries had said they told; their own part, it is likely, they omitted — and this made the hearers all the more courageous. He watches what follows with the same eye for propriety. These flee again to the true Succour, the invincible Alliance; and their prayers are framed with exquisite fitness: when they sought to be shown who was meet for the apostleship they addressed the one who knows the hearts of all men, prescience being wanted there, whereas here, where the mouths of adversaries needed stopping, they speak of lordship. To produce the prophecy is to sue God upon his own covenants, and at once to comfort themselves that all the imaginations of their foes are in vain. Barnes reads the report as a consultation: whether to obey the council and be silent, or to leave Jerusalem and preach elsewhere, was a real question, and they properly sought the counsel of their brethren and looked to God for direction, an example for all who are persecuted or perplexed about their duty. reformed Calvin gives two ends, that the others might be emboldened by the grace of God, and that they might arm themselves with prayer against the threatenings; so must the children of God do, pricking one another forward and joining hand in hand to vanquish the common adversary under Christ’s banner. They are to consider the dangers hanging over their heads, that they may be readier to face them, and to assure themselves of being invincible through the same power by which they got the victory before. He adds a caution about what is not recorded: the apostles, contented with the answer already given, probably did not contend further with those furious men, and yet we must persuade ourselves they did not so forget their former constancy as to submit to the ungodly decree like slaves. Henry adds a second purpose, that it might be recorded in the history of the church for posterity; Gill notes only the dismissal by the council’s own order.
24:
How a whole company uttered one prayer only one witness presses. grammatical-historical Ellicott says the phrase implies an intonation or chant unlike common speech, and sets out three ways it may be conceived: a direct inspiration giving all present the same words, the people following Peter clause by clause, or a hymn already familiar. He prefers the second, the hymn’s fitness for the occasion telling against the third, and the first assuming a miracle so startling that a more definite statement would be needed. Robertson reports a suggestion that the company sang the second Psalm and Peter then applied it, and calls the phrase a concert of voices. Barnes will not go so far: to lift up the voice was a Hebrew idiom for addressing a crowd, weeping, or prayer, and here it means simply that they prayed with one mind — a union still unbroken. The title they use all examine. Barnes explains that the word is not the usual one for Lord and that from it despot is derived: it carries absoluteness in ruling, where the commoner word denotes rather a property in a thing. Robertson notes it is the old word for a master’s relation to servants, and that Simeon addressed God so. Ellicott calls him the absolute Master of the Universe, and notes that a title seldom used of God in the New Testament recurs in the later writings of both apostles here. wesleyan-arminian Clarke paraphrases: thy rule is universal and thy power unlimited, heaven and earth and sea, with their endlessly varied inhabitants, being under thy control. Ellicott marks what the hymn is, the earliest recorded praise of the Christian Church, and thinks it significant that it begins as so many Psalms do, with the glory of God as Creator, rising to the redemptive work.

The second half of the prayer is a citation, and whom the Psalm concerns divides them five ways. reformed Gill reports the Jewish tradition: the psalm bears no title and no name, yet was reckoned David’s in the apostles’ time, and the ancient doctors of the synagogue held it to speak of the Messiah, though some read it of Gog and Magog. Barnes takes the quotation as proof, since it follows the Greek version exactly and the authority of the apostles settles the question; he sets aside the view that David composed it amid his own dangers, the more probable opinion being that it referred solely to the Messiah. Calvin will not give up the first sense. We must needs confess that David speaks of himself, he says, for after being anointed he came to the kingdom through the greatest difficulties, rulers and people conspiring against him and foreign enemies warring on a newly crowned man, so he complains with cause that the kings rage, and derides them because he knew God supported his kingdom. But because that kingdom was established to be a figure of Christ’s, David does not stay in the shadow: he apprehends the body. Clarke states the application without argument: the psalm relates to Christ and predicts the vain attempts of Jewish and heathen powers against Christianity. Ellicott approaches it as a lesson in the apostles’ school of prophetic interpretation: the psalm is not cited in the Gospels at all, what seems to us its most striking verse is passed over, and it is not referred to Christ until the Epistle to the Hebrews. Both he and Robertson note textual trouble in the introductory clause, and Robertson glosses the verb for raging as an untamed horse’s neighing. Wesley reduces the whole to a sentence: Lord, thou hast all power, and thy word is fulfilled; men rage against thee, but in vain. Calvin draws the rule for prayer: God’s power and his promise together are the two foundations of boldness, our prayers being acceptable only when, staying ourselves upon both, we pray in certain hope to obtain.
26:
That opposing Christ is opposing God, three witnesses draw independently. grammatical-historical Barnes takes opposition to the Messiah to be opposition to Jehovah, which the Scriptures uniformly suppose: he that neglects him neglects God, and he that despises him despises the one who sent him. reformed Calvin says the Spirit teaches that all make war against God who refuse to submit to Christ, though they little think it; since God will reign in his Son alone, we refuse to obey him as often as we rebel against Christ. Let hypocrites profess a thousand times that they mean nothing less than war against God, they shall find God their open enemy unless they embrace Christ with his gospel. The use is double, arming us against the terrors of the flesh, since those who withstand the gospel cannot vanquish God, and warning us not to advance against him to our own destruction. eastern-antiochene Cyril of Jerusalem turns the clause on those who confess one God but not the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, and who to this day rage against the Lord and his Anointed, thinking it possible to be friends of the Father apart from the Son, not knowing that no man comes to the Father but by him, who calls himself the Door and the Way: he who refuses the Way and denies the Door, how shall he be worthy of entrance unto God? On the word itself Clarke and Ellicott would translate rather than transliterate, rendering it against his Anointed, Clarke because it agrees with the verb following and Ellicott to keep the connection with the Psalm. Gill identifies the kings as the tetrarch of Galilee and the governor who represented Caesar; Barnes reads the two nouns as parallelism, not two classes but one idea twice stated, that men in authority of every kind would oppose the gospel.

The title given to Jesus next is the chief question. Barnes notes that the word rendered child is not the one commonly applied to the Lord Jesus and does not concern age, so son would be a happier translation. Ellicott renders it Servant, the very word used of David a verse earlier. reformed Gill takes it as child, the human nature being taken into union with the Son, unless it should rather be servant, a character often given Christ as Mediator; and presses the aggravation, that the man they rose against was holy in conception, birth and life. Calvin sees the ambiguity as deliberate. The Greeks use one word for servant and for son, and David bore it as the minister of God in ruling and in the prophetic office; it agrees better with the person of Christ, unless one prefers to say the writer alluded to David’s resemblance to Christ by setting down a word of double signification. Who the gathered parties were divides them. Barnes takes the Gentiles for the Romans and the people of Israel for the Jews stirred up by their rulers. Ellicott notes that neither noun has the article and that the plural peoples should, on Hebrew usage, be understood of Israel. Calvin asks why they are called Gentiles and people of Israel when there was but one body, and answers that diversity of countries is meant, Jews born in divers places making a concourse at the feast. On the added words in this city Lightfoot, Clarke and Ellicott agree that many manuscripts carry them, and Clarke thinks they make the sentence more emphatic; Lightfoot gives the reason they would be resisted: the Jews will not believe any rebellion against the Messiah could be raised in Jerusalem, referring the Psalm to Gog and Magog or some heathen country. Robertson observes that only this writer records the two rulers’ reconciliation at the trial, so the prayer treats the prophecy as fulfilled in their own conduct toward Jesus; Wesley says the anointing was to be king of Israel.
28:
The clause about the divine counsel raises the chapter’s hardest question, and gets five answers. wesleyan-arminian Clarke escapes by punctuation. There is a parenthesis here, not sufficiently noticed: the clause about the hand and counsel of God belongs not to the gatherers but to Christ. What God determined beforehand was not what Herod and Pilate and the rest were doing, for then their rage would be exactly what God had determined should take place, which is impious and absurd; rather they gathered to hinder what God had determined his Anointed should perform. reformed Calvin takes the opposite ground without flinching. God so governs all things by his secret counsel that he brings to pass what he has determined even by the wicked — not that they willingly do him such service, but because he turns their counsels backward, so that on one side appears righteousness and on the other only wickedness. Those who acknowledge God’s foreknowledge alone, without confessing that all things are done as it pleases him, are convicted by these words; and the writer, not content with one term, adds a second, to declare that events are not only governed by God’s counsel but ordered by his hand. When they rage fastest they may do only so much as is expedient to exercise us. Gill distinguishes intention from effect: it was not their design to fulfil God’s decrees but to satiate their malice, yet in the event, by the wise disposal of providence, their conspiracies brought about what God had decreed. Wesley reduces it to permission: they could do no more than God permitted, according to his counsel to save mankind by the sufferings of his Son. grammatical-historical Ellicott refuses to solve it at all. The great problem of the divine purpose and man’s free agency is stated here without any attempt at a philosophical solution, and none is possible: if we admit a divine will at all, we must follow the apostle and hold both facts, without seeking a logical formula of reconciliation. In every fact of history the will of each agent is free, and he stands or falls by the part he took; yet the outcome works out some increasing purpose we recognise only as we look back. That man proposes and God disposes is the nearest we can come to a practical, though not a theoretical, solution. Robertson says the praying company rise above sight and seem to see the Hand that shapes men’s ends.

What they ask follows from all this. Barnes notes what is absent from the petition: they did not purpose to abandon the undertaking but resolved to persevere, expecting danger, and asked not for safety but not to be deterred from speaking boldly. He observes too that opposite factions became united against the Messiah, and that the gospel meets the same opposition wherever preached. Clarke turns the petition outward: it is not against us but against thee that they conspire, not to stop our preaching but to bring thy counsel to nought. Calvin says they do well to extend to themselves what they cited of Christ, since he will not be separated from the gospel and takes to his own person whatever trouble befalls his members; and they ask that the cruelty of the adversaries be beaten down, not so much that they may live quietly as that they may have liberty to preach, it being not for them to desire a life spent idly. Robertson catches the irony: Peter and John had already defied the council, and all the same, and all the more, they pray for courage to match their brave words. Ellicott says the same: men who had shown boldness pray, conscious of their weakness, for a further bestowal of the gift. Gill reads the request that God behold the threatenings as asking such notice as would rebuke or restrain them, or make his servants fearless.
30:
The petition asks for more of what has already cost them dearly. reformed Calvin puts the question directly: seeing one miracle had stung the enemy so sore, how do these holy men desire new miracles daily? The answer is that they make so great account of the glory of God that in comparison they set light by all else, having respect to this one thing only, that the power of God may be declared — which the godly ought always to desire, though the adversaries burst and all hell rage. He draws a rule from it, that we rightly acknowledge God’s benefits only when they prick us forward to pray that he will confirm what he has begun; the apostles had shown heroic fortitude, and now pray again for boldness, as Paul asked the faithful to pray that his mouth might be opened when his voice already sounded everywhere. grammatical-historical Barnes notes what the prayer omits: they did not even ask that God preserve their lives or keep them from danger, but sought the continuance of miracles as evidence of the truth of what they delivered. Ellicott hears an intentional assonance in the Greek between the word for healing and the name of Jesus, as though the name itself witnessed to his being the great Healer, and would render the title Servant rather than child, as Clarke does, it being the word used of David a few verses earlier. wesleyan-arminian Clarke frames the request as an appeal: show that it is thy truth we proclaim, and how highly thou hast magnified thy Son, whom they have despised and crucified. Gill adds that such healing would cross the schemes of the council, confirm the doctrines of the Gospel and animate the preachers; Robertson notes that God’s hand is named a second time in one prayer, and that what they ask is visible proof that God has heard their request for courage even unto death.

The answer comes at once, and the sign divides them. Barnes says the word for shaking denotes violent agitation and is fitted to express an earthquake, and gives four reasons why they took it for an answer: it was sudden and not from natural causes, it came while they sought direction, it was an exhibition of great power, and a convulsion so mighty was fitted to awe them — Jews and heathen alike, he adds, regarding an earthquake as a token of the deity’s presence. Robertson agrees an earthquake is most likely, and none the less a token of God’s presence. Ellicott reads the impression on the senses as a renewal of Pentecost, but without the tongues of fire, which were symbols of a gift imparted once for all, and perhaps without the marvel of tongues besides; the disciples felt the power of the Spirit, sense confirming inward consciousness, and it came in the form for which they had specially prayed. Calvin will not let the sign carry the weight. The shaking should of itself have done them small good, being nothing but a token that God is present; the fruit follows, that they were filled with the Holy Ghost and endowed with greater boldness, and on this second member we ought rather to stand — for the shaking was rare and extraordinary, whereas obtaining what was asked is the perpetual profit of prayer, set before us for an example. Clarke draws from the filling that though they had the Spirit at Pentecost they were capable of larger communications, one always making way for another: God gives grace for the time being but no stock for futurity, because he will keep his followers continually dependent on himself, and had these disciples relied on their pentecostal grace they might have sunk under the terror of their foes. Wesley says the petition was granted; Robertson observes that the writer describes their conduct in the very words of their prayer.
32:
The unity is stated in two words, and both are weighed. grammatical-historical Ellicott distinguishes them on Hebrew usage, heart for the intellectual side of character and soul for the emotional, though the two overlap and are set together to express the whole without minute analysis. Robertson objects that the English is curiously unlike the Greek, which has a nominative not a genitive: there was one heart and soul in the multitude of believers. Barnes and Clarke both recall the ancient definition of a friend as one soul in two bodies, and Clarke asks what that philosopher would have thought had he seen one soul in five thousand bodies. puritan-evangelical Henry dwells on how unlikely it was. Many of very different ages, tempers and conditions, strangers before they believed, were now as intimately acquainted as if they had known one another for years; some had been of different sects, or had had civil quarrels, and these were laid aside — the blessed fruit of Christ’s dying precept that they love one another and his prayer that they all might be one. He adds that the increase of the church is its glory, the multitude of believers more than their quality. reformed Calvin marvels at the number: where faith bears the chief sway it so knits the hearts of men that all both will and nill one thing, discord springing up only because we are not all governed by the same Spirit; and since the wicked also conspire, this concord was holy because it was among the faithful. Gill counts the believers at about eight thousand.

What the community of goods amounted to is the second question. Ellicott says the form of expression implies it was not compulsory: the goods still belonged to men, but they did not speak of them as their own, thinking of themselves not as possessors but as stewards, so the rights of property, though not abolished, were by their owners’ spontaneous action made subservient to the law of love, without the nicely calculated less or more of a later time. Robertson makes the distinction shorter: common in use, not in possession, as the writer proceeds to explain. Wesley grounds it wholly in the affection: none could call his goods his own while all were of one soul, and so long as that Christian love continued they could not but have all things common. Calvin sets out the order: inward unity goes before as the root and the fruit follows, so we must love one another with sincere affection and then that love must show itself in external effects, since a beneficence not rising from the heart is nothing before God, while in vain do we boast of right affection unless some testimony appears in outward offices. On the witness and the grace, Barnes reads the power as belonging to their preaching rather than their miracles, since the resurrection was the point to be established and all Christ taught rested on it, and takes the grace as favour with the people won largely by their liberality — nothing inclining men to the gospel like kindness that ministers to their temporal wants, which softens the heart and disarms prejudice. Calvin says it in a phrase, that they were beloved because beneficent, though their honesty and patience doubtless won goodwill too. Clarke will have the word carry both senses, since they received much of the favour of God and much favour with all who feared God, his benevolence never being exerted without his beneficence. Ellicott declines to choose between the grace of God bestowed in full measure and the favour of the people, no sufficient data existing for a decision. Robertson notes they kept giving their witness after the answer to their prayer, on the very issue for which they were arrested; Gill takes the power for fervency of spirit, efficacy on souls, or the working of miracles.
34:
Whether the selling was universal is the chief question. grammatical-historical Barnes says the phrase is large and indefinite, and it would be improper to press it into meaning that every individual sold all at once: they parted with whatever was needed to supply the poor. That it was no obligation is plain from the case of Ananias, and the singling out of one man by name shows it was not universal. reformed Calvin reaches the same conclusion by the same road. Though the speech is universal it is all one as if indefinite, and many are to be thought not to have diminished their possessions; nor did the faithful sell all they had, but only so much as need required, the words being amplification, to say that the rich relieved their brethren not merely out of the revenue of their lands but did not spare the lands themselves. He adds that they used great wisdom, the distribution being made as every man had need, so the goods were divided not equally but discreetly, lest any be oppressed with poverty. Gill notes what the practice bought them: such care of their poor was a reason why they stood in so much favour with the people. wesleyan-arminian Clarke supplies a historical cause: it had been customary to call the poor together to eat of the sacrifices, but with the priests incensed against Christianity the Christian poor had no such advantage, so a common stock supplied them — a provision which could be but temporary, made suitably and seasonably. Wesley draws the opposite inference, that the freedom from want is added as proof that great grace was upon them all: there was no particular command, but there was great grace and great love, of which this was the natural fruit, and in all ages the same grace could not but in like circumstances produce the same effect.

Why land in particular was sold draws a striking suggestion. Ellicott notes that both verbs imply continuous action, and thinks that besides the impulse of love they may have been impressed by their Lord’s warnings of coming troubles with the instability of earthly possessions, landed property in Palestine being then more a source of anxiety than profit. As the prophet showed his faith in the future restoration of his people by buying the field at Anathoth, so there was in this selling of estates a proof of faith in the desolation their Master had foretold. Barnes offers a plainer reason: they were about to go to other lands to preach and were leaving their native country. Robertson keeps the tenses in view: selling, they brought as need arose, so the wants were kept supplied. On the laying at the apostles’ feet Ellicott gives a picture of Eastern life, since gifts made to a king or priest or teacher are not placed in his hands but at his feet, the apostles appearing to sit in conclave on their twelve seats. Gill reads the gesture as veneration for the apostles and a kind of contempt for their own worldly substance; Clarke as showing how cordially they parted with it, and as entrusting the management to men to whom God had entrusted the gifts of his Spirit. Barnes notes that this soon became a burdensome office, so men were afterwards appointed to have especial charge of it; Robertson that the distribution went on as any one had need. Calvin ends on a rebuke: no man had his own privately to himself that he alone might enjoy it, neglecting others, but as need required they were ready to bestow upon all — and we must needs have more than iron bowels, seeing we are no more moved by this history, since the faithful then gave abundantly of what was their own, while we are not content to suppress wickedly what is in our hands but rob others besides.
36:
Why one man is named out of so many gets three answers. eastern-antiochene Chrysostom reads it as deliberate arrangement. The writer is about to relate the affair of Ananias and Sapphira, and to show that man’s sin at its worst he first mentions the one who performed the virtuous deed: there being so great a multitude all doing the same, so great grace and so great miracles, and he, taught by none of these but blinded by covetousness, brought destruction on his own head. grammatical-historical Barnes gives three reasons of another kind — that he was a foreigner, that his was a remarkable instance of liberality, and that he afterwards distinguished himself in the ministry — and traces his course with Paul until they parted over Mark and he sailed for Cyprus. Robertson takes him as one illustration of those who sold and brought the money, and infers from the singling out that all did not actually sell but were ready if needed. How a Levite came to own land is the other question. Lightfoot supposes the surname distinguished two noted men of one name; reformed Gill will not say whether the land lay in Cyprus or Judea nor how it was got, whether by purchase, as a priest once bought a field at Anathoth, or as his wife’s dowry, since the Levites had nothing by inheritance but their cities and suburb fields, never to be sold — though that law was now abolished, and the Jewish doctors read the prohibition of exchanging rather than selling. wesleyan-arminian Clarke answers more simply: the Levites as a tribe had no land but individuals might purchase anywhere, and this man’s probably lay in Cyprus, sold perhaps to countrymen up at the feast. Ellicott agrees that nothing hindered a priest or Levite from possessing land by purchase or inheritance, though the original polity gave them land in common and no private property; Wesley states only the rule, that a Levite had no distinct inheritance in Israel.

What the new name means is the second question, and the answers differ. Barnes derives it from two Syriac words as son of prophecy, the Greek used to interpret it meaning exhortation though translated consolation. Clarke argues from the distinction the New Testament draws between exhortation and consolation that the original was son of prophecy or exhortation, and that this was the way the man afterwards distinguished himself. Ellicott takes it literally as son of prophecy on the Hebrew etymology, or son of counsel on the writer’s translation, and reads it as a gift of persuasive utterance in which the apostles recognised the work of the Spirit: the Paraclete had endowed him with the gift of paraclesis, a word including counsel, comfort, admonition and the application of divine truth to men’s necessities. Robertson makes encouragement the chief idea and alone doubts the derivation: it is not necessary to think the apostles coined the name, since it may have come from a form meaning son of Nebo, or the Hebrew for son of a prophet — but whatever its origin, the popular sense is what the writer gives. Wesley refers the title both to his assisting the poor with his fortune and to the gifts by which he was qualified to comfort and exhort. Clarke adds what none of the others make: the two apostles of the Gentiles, though of Jewish extraction, were both born in Gentile countries, which removed prejudice from the heathen and gave them a facility in Greek without which they could have done little in the Roman empire. Ellicott supposes an earlier acquaintance behind their friendship, perhaps schooling in the same place or the same early practice of the craft they later worked at together, and reports the tradition that made him one of the Seventy. Gill notes the name is only a contraction, the surname distinguishing this man from another who bore it.
